summary: A concrete light on a sunk crib at the Lake Superior end of the St. Marys River, after twenty-nine years of lightship service; reached by boat only.

structures.note: Concrete superstructure on a sunk crib with an ice-breaking prow (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett). The CCG list gives a white tower 18.3 m high.
Keepers' residence on the crib (LighthouseFriends: two-tier; Rowlett: three-story)

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property. Tower closed. Accessible only by boat (Rowlett). The CCG list marks the light Seasonal.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1923 date is when lightvessel No. 22 went on station (Lake Carriers' Association, as quoted by LighthouseFriends). The 1953 date is the concrete light on its crib. The record's two first-year values are both right for different structures; the station's light was a ship until about 1952.

The Canadian Coast Guard's List of Lights gives Fl W 10s for entry 1081, the current light. Rowlett's directory gives a red flash every 5 s with a focal plane of 18 m (59 ft). The Wikidata value Fl R 5s recorded in the database matches Rowlett, not the CCG list or LighthouseFriends. The sources disagree and the story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Shape: the record's kind is lighthouse, so the story uses the light-station headings; the lightship years are in Building the light and The keepers. Lit date is disputed: LighthouseFriends gives completion in 1953, but the 9 December 1952 Evening News it quotes says the new light had been in temporary service for about three weeks, and the SooToday column says the crib came up the Soo Locks on 25 August 1952. Both are recorded. Length of St. Julien: 130 ft (LighthouseFriends) against 140 ft (SooToday); both are in the story. Characteristic: the CCG list says Fl W 10s; Rowlett's directory says a red flash every 5 s with a focal plane of 18 m (59 ft); Wikipedia (not cited) says Fl R 5s. The story reports the disagreement. The column's McKiggan line is indirect speech ("McKiggan reported that..."), so the story attributes it to the column, not to McKiggan. Structure: the CCG list gives a white tower 18.3 m; Rowlett and the Wikipedia article describe the light on the roof of a three-story keeper's quarters; both are reported without reconciling. The 1908 casualty entry (tug Philadelphia at North Gros Cap, 3 October 1907) is near the reef but is not tied to it by any source; it is in the story as context, not as a station event. The Lake Carriers' Association report, the Evening News of 9 December 1952 and Ripley's 1899 statement are quoted only as LighthouseFriends quotes them; none was read directly. The Canadian report quotes are from the Department's works lists read from the Internet Archive text; the printed page for scan p. 111 is uncertain (printed p. 104?), so the story cites scan pages. The captains' and keepers' names are spelled as each source spells them (Griffith in LighthouseFriends, Griffiths in the column). Gavin McKiggan and Marvin Moreau are named only as the column names them, in their public role, with no dates or personal detail. The record's photo (a Commons image of a grounded vessel, Roger Blough, on Lake Superior) does not show this station; it is flagged here for the editor, not as a correction field. No photos were added.

corrections.why: The file title describes a US Coast Guard response to a grounded freighter in Lake Superior, not this light. LighthouseFriends' photographs are copyright and were not reused.
